Share price divided by earnings per share: how many years of today's profit the price pays for.
Price over the earnings analysts expect for the next twelve months; flattered when forecasts are too high.
Price over the ten-year average of inflation-adjusted earnings (Campbell and Shiller); smooths the cycle and predicts ten-year returns far better than one-year returns.
nodes.f: CAPE = real price / mean(real EPS over 10 years)

nodes.t: The CAPE earnings yield (1/CAPE) minus the real ten-year yield: the extra return stocks offer over inflation-protected bonds.
Earnings per share over price, the inverse of P/E; comparable to a bond yield.
P/E divided by expected growth in percent; Lynch's rough check that a growth company is not overpriced for its growth.
Enterprise value over earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; compares firms with different debt.
Enterprise value over revenue; used when profits are small or distorted.
Price over accounting equity per share; the classic value metric, weaker where assets are intangible.
Annual dividends over price; once a strong predictor of returns, weaker since buybacks replaced dividends.
Dividends plus net buybacks over market value: total cash returned to owners.
Free cash flow over market value; cash, not accounting profit, that the business could hand back.
Buffett's measure: net income plus depreciation minus the capex needed just to keep the business where it is.
Value as the sum of future cash flows, each divided by (1 + discount rate) for every year of waiting.
Solving a DCF backwards: the growth a price already assumes, which can then be checked against how often companies achieve it.
The revenue or earnings growth a price needs to be fair; the engine's main test of irrational pricing.
How often companies of a given size have achieved a given growth rate historically; the outside view on a forecast.
The value of all cash flows after the forecast years; often most of a DCF, which makes long-duration stocks rate sensitive.
The return required to wait for cash; the risk-free rate plus a risk premium.
The blend of the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, weighted by how the firm is funded.
nodes.f: WACC = E/V re + D/V rd (1 - t)

nodes.t: What shareholders require: the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium in the CAPM.
The extra return investors expect from stocks over safe bonds; low when stocks are expensive relative to yields.
Comparing the stock earnings yield with the ten-year Treasury yield; popular but criticized for mixing a real and a nominal yield (Asness 2003).
Total stock market value over GDP; Buffett's 2001 rough gauge of how expensive the market is.
Market value of firms over the cost of replacing their assets; above one invites building more.
How much investors pay for a unit of profit or cash across the market; high levels mean lower long-run returns on average.
The average return a rational investor anticipates; not a forecast of any one year.
What a business is worth to an owner from its future cash, independent of the quote today.
Buying well below estimated value so errors in the estimate do not cost money (Graham).
After-tax operating profit over the capital tied up to earn it; growth creates value only when ROIC exceeds the cost of capital.
Net income over shareholders' equity; inflated by leverage and buybacks.
A durable advantage (scale, network effects, switching costs, brand, patents) that keeps returns above the cost of capital.
Returns that come from investors paying more per unit of earnings, not from earnings growth; it reverses.
Changes in analysts' forecasts; rising estimates tend to lead prices for a while.
Consensus forecasts of earnings; historically too optimistic a year out.
Net income divided by shares outstanding; buybacks raise it without raising profit.
The rate profits rise; over long periods it tracks nominal GDP for the market as a whole.
Buying assets for less than they are worth on fundamentals (Graham, Buffett, Klarman).
Paying up for companies whose earnings should compound fast for long; works when growth persists.
How sensitive a stock's value is to the discount rate; far-off cash flows mean long duration, like a long bond.
Valuing each business line separately and adding them, often revealing a conglomerate discount.
Market value of equity plus debt minus cash: the price of the whole business.
The tendency of stretched quantities (valuations, margins, volatility) to drift back toward their long-run average.
Dividends over earnings.
A company repurchasing its own stock; returns cash and raises EPS, and is a steady buyer in the market.
Assets minus liabilities on the balance sheet.
The yield on government bills or bonds, the return for waiting without default risk; the base of every discount rate.
The interest rate a company pays to borrow, after the tax saving on interest.
The cash a business would produce if it stopped growing: revenue less costs and the capex needed only to maintain it.
Mauboussin and Rappaport's method: read the expectations a price implies, then judge whether they are likely to be revised.
The rhythm of expansion and recession; earnings, credit and commodity demand all ride it.
A breakdown in funding and trust that forces selling across markets at once.
The slow move by some reserve managers and trade partners away from the dollar, visible mainly in central bank gold buying.
The US Energy Information Administration's weekly inventory data and monthly Short-Term Energy Outlook.
One series moving before another; useful for forecasting only if it survives out of sample.
The exchange of cash and securities after a trade; US stocks settle the next business day.
What an asset earns if prices do not move: a bond's yield over funding, a currency's rate gap, a commodity's roll; it predicts returns across asset classes (Koijen et al. 2018).
Sales recognized in the period; the top line every margin is measured against.
The rules for when a sale counts as revenue; aggressive timing pulls future sales forward.
Revenue minus the direct cost of goods, over revenue; pricing power shows up here first.
Operating income over revenue.
Net income over revenue.
How much profit rises for a rise in sales when costs are fixed; cuts both ways.
Revenue, costs and profit over a period.
What a company owns and owes at a point in time.
Cash from operations, investing and financing; harder to flatter than earnings.
Cash generated by the business in the period, before investment.
Operating cash flow minus capital spending: cash left for owners.
Spending on long-lived assets such as data centres, fabs and power plants.
The spending needed just to keep capacity where it is; often approximated by depreciation.
Spreading an asset's cost over its useful life; a short life lowers profits now, a long one flatters them.
The years over which an asset is depreciated; servers set at five to six years when the economic life may be shorter.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; ignores the cost of the assets that earn it.
EBITDA with management's chosen exclusions; read the adjustments.
Earnings that exclude items management calls unusual, often including stock pay; higher than GAAP by design.
US Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the audited standard.
Pay in shares; a real cost to owners through dilution even though it uses no cash.
Earnings not yet backed by cash; high accruals predict lower future returns (Sloan 1996).
Operating cash flow over net income; below one means profits are not turning into cash.
How well reported profit reflects durable cash generation.
Receivables and inventory minus payables; swings in it move cash without moving profit.
Cash collected before the service is delivered; flatters cash flow while it grows.
Goods held for sale; a build-up can signal weak demand or a coming price war.
The premium paid in an acquisition over the fair value of net assets; written down when the deal sours.
A write-down when an asset is worth less than its book value.
Debt minus cash.
Net debt over EBITDA, a lender's first measure of how stretched a borrower is.
Operating income over interest expense.
Long-term rental commitments, now on the balance sheet; data-centre leases are large and long.
Obligations kept outside the reported balance sheet through vehicles or guarantees.
The average of the last n prices, updated each period; smooths noise to show the trend.
An equal-weighted moving average.
A moving average that weights recent prices more, with weight 2/(n+1) on the newest.
The average of the last 200 trading days (about ten months); price above it is the most common definition of an uptrend.
The average of the last 50 trading days; the medium-term trend.
Hold stocks when the monthly price is above its ten-month average, else cash (Faber 2007); the engine tests it on 155 years.
The 50-day average crossing above (golden) or below (death) the 200-day.
Wilder's 0 to 100 gauge of recent gains against losses over 14 periods; above 70 is called overbought, below 30 oversold.
Labels for prices that have risen or fallen fast; on their own they rarely predict reversals in trending markets.
Appel's moving average convergence divergence: the 12-period EMA minus the 26-period EMA, against its own 9-period EMA.
A 20-period average with bands two standard deviations above and below; band width tracks volatility.
Wilder's measure of daily range including gaps; used to size stops.
Wilder's average directional index: trend strength, not direction.
Where the close sits within the recent high-low range, 0 to 100.
A running total of volume signed by the day's direction.
Volume-weighted average price over a session; an execution benchmark as much as an indicator.
Shares or contracts traded; conviction behind a move.
Price levels where buying or selling has gathered before; self-fulfilling when many watch them.
A move through support or resistance or to a new high.
The year's extreme prices; stocks near highs tend to keep doing better (George and Hwang 2004).
Buying what has risen and selling what has fallen over months, across many markets; paid in crises (Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen 2017).
The tendency of recent winners to keep winning for months (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993).
An asset's own past year return predicting its next month (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012).
Trend followers' habit of making money in long sell-offs.
Price making a new high while an oscillator does not; a warning, not a signal.
How many stocks share in a move; narrow rallies led by a few giants are fragile.
Running total of advancing minus declining stocks.
A breadth gauge of the trend under the index surface.
Put volume over call volume; extremes read as fear or greed.
Levels at 38.2, 50 and 61.8 percent of a move; widely used, without reliable evidence.
The fall from the previous peak; the loss that tests whether an investor can stay invested.
Finding a rule that worked by trying many; its backtest overstates its future (Sullivan, Timmermann and White 1999).
The rise in the general price level; erodes cash and bonds and decides what the Fed does.
The BLS index of consumer prices; the headline inflation measure.
Inflation without food and energy; the Fed's guide to the trend.
The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
The overnight rate the central bank sets (the fed funds rate in the US).
A guide that sets the policy rate from inflation's gap to target and output's gap to potential.
How far the economy runs above or below its potential.
Central bank bond buying to push down long rates and add reserves.
Letting the central bank's bonds roll off; drains reserves.
The ease of funding and trading; ample liquidity props up risk assets, scarce liquidity breaks them.
Banks' deposits at the Fed; the system's cash.
Where money funds park cash at the Fed; once it is empty, drains come out of reserves.
An index of how easy credit, equity and dollar conditions are (Chicago Fed NFCI).
The value of everything an economy produces; nominal GDP growth bounds long-run profit growth.
A broad, lasting fall in activity; earnings fall, defaults rise, and stocks typically drop a third.
Inflation falling without a recession.
High inflation with weak growth; the worst regime for a stock and bond portfolio.
The share of the labour force without work.
A recession signal when the three-month average unemployment rate rises half a point above its prior-year low.
Monthly US job gains; the market's most-watched data release.
Government spending above revenue; financed by issuing bonds.
The stock of bonds a government owes; its interest cost rises with rates.
The amount of new duration the market must absorb, from Treasuries and corporate issuers.
The world's reserve and funding currency; a strong dollar tightens global conditions and weighs on commodities and gold.
Taxes on imports; raise prices and can lower growth.
Output per hour; the only lasting source of higher real wages and margins.
The rise in pay; feeds services inflation.
Cash and deposits in the economy.
A sudden jump in oil prices from lost supply; raises inflation and lowers growth.
Currencies' prices against each other; set by rate gaps, growth, flows and risk appetite.
Borrowing in a low-rate currency to hold a high-rate one; earns slowly and loses fast in crises.
The benchmark long-term rate; it sets mortgage rates and the discount rate on long-duration stocks.
Yields on bills and two-year notes; follow expected policy rates.
Yields by maturity; its slope reflects expected policy and the term premium.
Short rates above long rates; historically preceded most US recessions with a long, variable lag.
Trades on the curve's slope widening or narrowing.
The extra yield for locking money up long instead of rolling short bills; rises with supply and inflation uncertainty.
The yield after inflation, observed on TIPS; the true cost of money.
Nominal yield minus the TIPS yield: the inflation the bond market prices.
Treasury bonds whose principal rises with CPI.
The percentage change in a bond's price for a one-point change in yield; long bonds have high duration.
How duration itself changes with yield; long bonds gain more when yields fall than they lose when they rise.
Moves opposite the yield.
An ETF of 20+ year Treasuries; the book's classic hedge, which fails when stocks and bonds fall together.
What a bond earns if yields do not move: its coupon over funding plus the price gain as it rolls down the curve.
The extra yield on corporate debt over Treasuries; widens before and during stress.
Bonds rated below investment grade; behave half like stocks.
The weakest rated borrowers; cracks show here first.
Bonds rated BBB- or better.
Failure to pay; default rates rise in recessions and when rates stay high for borrowers who refinance.
What creditors get back after a default.
Insurance against a borrower's default, quoted as an annual spread.
Investors who sell government bonds to punish fiscal excess, pushing yields up.
Implied volatility of Treasury options; the VIX of bonds.
The gap between swap rates and Treasury yields; negative when dealers' balance sheets are full.
How new debt is sold; weak demand (tails, low bid-to-cover) moves yields.
The right, not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) at a set price before a date.
The right to buy at the strike; pays when the price rises above it.
The right to sell at the strike; insurance against a fall.
Buying one put and selling a lower one: cheaper insurance that stops paying below the lower strike.
Buying a put and selling a call: free or cheap protection that gives up gains above the call.
Selling calls against stock held: income that caps upside.
Buying (or selling) both a call and a put: a bet on (or against) a big move.
The 1973 formula that prices a European option from spot, strike, time, rates and volatility.
nodes.f: C = S N(d1) - K e^(-rT) N(d2)

nodes.t: The volatility that makes the option price fit Black-Scholes; the market's priced uncertainty.
The volatility prices actually showed; usually below implied, which pays option sellers on average.
Implied minus realized variance; the insurance premium option sellers collect, and lose in crashes.
Downside puts priced at higher implied volatility than calls: crash insurance demand.
Cboe's 30-day implied volatility of the S&P 500; the fear gauge.
Option sensitivities: delta (to price), gamma (delta's change), vega (to volatility), theta (to time), rho (to rates).
How much dealers must buy or sell as prices move to stay hedged; negative gamma amplifies moves.
Options expiring the same day; now a large share of S&P 500 option volume.
Call minus put equals spot minus the discounted strike; arbitrage keeps them aligned.
Exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell later at a price agreed now, marked to market daily.
A private agreement to trade later at a set price.
Spot minus futures; converges to zero at expiry.
Collateral posted against a leveraged position; margin calls force selling in falls.
A position that gains when the main bet loses; it costs something on average.
Cheap, far out-of-the-money protection that pays only in crashes (Spitznagel, Taleb).
Raw materials traded in bulk: energy, metals, grains, softs and livestock.
How most investors hold commodities; returns come from spot, roll and collateral (Gorton and Rouwenhorst 2006).
Futures above spot, usually when inventories are ample; rolling long positions loses money.
Futures below spot, usually when supply is tight; long positions earn as they roll.
The gain or loss from replacing an expiring future with the next; positive in backwardation.
The benefit of holding the physical commodity when supply is short (Kaldor, Working).
Futures equal spot plus financing and storage minus convenience yield; low inventories mean backwardation.
Financing plus storage costs of holding a commodity until a future date.
Keynes's idea that hedgers pay speculators a premium, so futures sit below the expected spot price.
Stocks of oil, gas, metals or grain; the buffer that sets the curve's shape.
The producers' group that sets output quotas; its spare capacity caps price spikes.
Production that can be added quickly; low spare capacity makes prices jumpy.
The US government's emergency oil stock.
The North Sea benchmark for most of the world's oil.
The US benchmark, delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma.
The gap between the two benchmarks; cointegrated, with deviations that close over weeks.
The refining margin: product prices minus crude.
Soybean meal and oil value minus soybean cost: the crusher's margin.
Power price minus the gas cost to make it: the gas plant's margin.
Henry Hub in the US, TTF in Europe, LNG in Asia; strongly seasonal and storage driven.
Gas cooled to liquid and shipped; links regional gas markets, a fifth of it through Hormuz.
A store of value with no yield; driven by real yields, the dollar, fear and central bank buying.
Reserve managers buying gold to diversify away from dollars; a steady bid since 2022.
Half precious metal, half industrial input.
The industrial metal of wiring and grids; Dr. Copper for its read on growth, and a data-centre input.
Currencies of exporters (AUD, CAD, NOK, BRL, ZAR) that move with their commodities.
Steel's raw material; China's construction cycle sets its price.
China consumes about half the world's metals; its credit cycle drives the metals cycle.
Wheat, corn, soybeans and their oils; weather and stocks-to-use drive prices.
The USDA's monthly world supply and demand estimates for crops.
Coffee, cocoa, sugar, cotton: tropical crops prone to weather shocks.
The CFTC's weekly breakdown of futures positions by trader type; extremes in speculators' positions mark crowded trades.
The old saying that stocks do better from November to April than from May to October; the engine tests it since 1871 and since 1950.
Regular calendar patterns: gas peaks in winter, grains around harvest; in stocks, mostly folklore.
A decade-long price boom from a demand surge meeting slow supply.
The shift to electricity and renewables; raises demand for copper, power and gas backup.
The chokepoint for about a fifth of world oil and LNG; its closure in 2026 is the book's live oil shock.
The gap between the best buy and sell quotes; the toll for immediacy.
How much can trade without moving the price; vanishes when needed most.
Resting limit orders at each price.
An order to trade only at a set price or better; may not fill.
An order to trade now at the best available price; certain fill, uncertain price.
An order that becomes a market order when a price is hit; can fill far away in a gap.
The difference between the expected and actual fill price.
How much a trade moves the price against itself; grows with the square root of size (the square-root law).
Impact scales with the square root of the order's share of daily volume, across markets.
Trading a large order fast (more impact) or slow (more price risk) optimally (2000).
Turning a decision into fills at low cost: slicing, timing, venue choice.
Time-weighted average price: an even pace of trading.
The cost from decision price to final fill, including what never filled.
How far price moves per unit of order flow when informed traders hide among noise traders (Kyle 1985).
Trading against someone who knows more; the reason spreads exist (Glosten and Milgrom 1985).
A dealer who quotes both sides and earns the spread while managing inventory and adverse selection.
A dealer's exposure to positions accumulated while making markets.
Automated trading at microsecond speed, mostly market making and arbitrage.
Delay between a signal and an order reaching the market.
Wholesalers paying brokers for retail orders, which they fill inside the spread.
Venues without public quotes; a large share of US volume trades off exchange.
A large trade negotiated privately and printed at once, often at a discount.
Borrowing shares to sell, hoping to buy back cheaper; losses are unbounded.
Shorts forced to buy as prices rise, driving prices higher.
The fee to borrow shares to short.
A demand for more collateral; forced selling begets more selling.
Borrowing to hold more than one's capital; magnifies gains, losses and the risk of being forced out.
Cutting positions to reduce leverage, often all at once.
Exchange-wide trading halts after large falls.
US stocks settle one business day after trade since 2024.
Authorized participants swap baskets for ETF shares, keeping prices near NAV.
Forced buying and selling when index weights change.
Individual investors' share of trading; surges in manias.
Profiting from a price gap between equivalent assets; limited by capital and risk (Shleifer and Vishny 1997).
Commissions, spreads, impact and taxes; they turn many backtested edges negative.
How much of a portfolio trades each year.
The standard deviation of returns; the most common, and incomplete, measure of risk.
How much an asset moves with the market; the CAPM's measure of risk that cannot be diversified away.
Return beyond what the asset's risk exposures explain; mostly luck after costs (Fama and French 2010).
Sharpe's 1964 model: expected return rises only with beta.
How two returns move together, from -1 to 1; it rises in crises, when diversification is needed most.
Positive when inflation drives both; then bonds stop hedging stocks.
How often assets crash together; correlation understates it.
Holding assets that do not move together to lower risk without lowering expected return.
Too much in one name, sector or factor; the AI book's defining risk.
Excess return over volatility; the standard risk-adjusted score.
Like Sharpe but counts only downside volatility.
The worst peak-to-trough loss; the number that ends careers and funds.
The loss not exceeded with a given confidence over a horizon; silent about the tail beyond it.
The average loss beyond the VaR; describes the tail.
Extreme moves far more often than a bell curve allows; kurtosis above 3.
A rare, extreme, unforeseen event that is explained only afterwards (Taleb).
The bet size that maximizes long-run growth: edge over odds; full Kelly is wild, half Kelly is common.
The chance of losing the whole bankroll; falls exponentially with bankroll over variance.
How much to put in each bet; more important than which bets.
A rule to exit after a set loss; limits damage, adds whipsaw.
Returning weights to target; sells winners and buys losers.
Weighting assets so each adds equal risk, usually with leverage on bonds (Bridgewater's All Weather).
60% stocks and 40% bonds; it suffered its worst year in 2022 as both fell.
How much hedge per unit of exposure; the minimum-variance ratio is the regression slope.
Tilting toward characteristics with long-run premia: value, momentum, quality, size, low volatility, carry.
Cheap stocks beating expensive ones over long periods; it suffered a lost decade to 2020.
Profitable, stable, low-debt companies earning more than their risk suggests.
Low-risk stocks earning as much as high-risk ones.
The book's loss in a chosen bad scenario.
Weighing a few coherent futures instead of one forecast.
Many funds in the same trade; exits become stampedes.
A period with its own rules (low inflation, high inflation, crisis); links and hedges change between them.
Active return over tracking error.
Fitting a line (or plane) through data to measure how one variable moves with others.
The regression that minimizes squared errors.
The share of variation a model explains in-sample; flattering.
How much better a model forecasts than the historical mean on data it never saw (Campbell and Thompson 2008).
The chance of a result at least this extreme if nothing were going on; not the chance the idea is wrong.
An estimate over its standard error; above 3 is the modern bar for a new factor (Harvey, Liu and Zhu 2016).
How much an estimate would vary across samples.
Standard errors that allow for autocorrelation and changing volatility (1987).
Resampling the data to see how much an estimate could vary (Efron 1979).
Resampling blocks of random length to keep time dependence (Politis and Romano 1994).
Running many tests guarantees some false positives; Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections adjust for it.
A step-down correction that controls the chance of any false positive.
The expected share of false findings among those declared (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).
A model that fits noise; great in-sample, poor after.
How often the in-sample winner falls to the bottom half out of sample (Bailey et al. 2017).
A Sharpe ratio adjusted for how many strategies were tried and for fat tails (Bailey and Lopez de Prado 2014).
Judging a model only on data it was not built on.
Using information in a backtest that was not available at the time.
Studying only what survived (funds, stocks) and so overstating returns.
Monthly averages of prices create spurious autocorrelation of about 0.25 (Working 1960), flattering trend rules on averaged data.
A series whose statistical behaviour does not drift; prices are not, returns roughly are.

nodes.n: Unit root and the ADF test
nodes.t: Testing whether a series wanders like a random walk (Dickey and Fuller 1979).
Two wandering series tied by a long-run relationship; their spread mean-reverts (Engle and Granger 1987).
Betting on the spread of two related assets returning to normal.
Whether one series' past improves forecasts of another; prediction, not proof of cause.
Telling cause from correlation: experiments, natural experiments, or structural assumptions stated out loud.
A hidden common cause that makes two things move together; the robustness value says how strong it would have to be.
The share of variance an unseen confounder must explain to erase an estimate (Cinelli and Hazlett 2020).
Learning causal direction from non-Gaussian data: the cause is the variable whose residuals look independent of it (Shimizu et al. 2006).
What would have happened had one cause been different, holding the rest.
Each series regressed on the past of all; impulse responses trace a shock through time.
The path of every series after a one-time shock to one.
The share of forecast-error variance coming from other variables' shocks (Diebold and Yilmaz 2012).
Shocks spreading across markets beyond what fundamentals justify.
Estimating which variables are linked once all others are held fixed, with most links set to zero.
Correlation after removing what other variables explain.
Keeping only what survives refits on many half-samples, with a bound on false findings.
Tracking a hidden quantity that drifts, updating with each observation.
A model in which the data switch between hidden regimes with fixed probabilities (Hamilton 1989).
Volatility that clusters: today's variance depends on yesterday's shock and variance (Bollerslev 1986).
Answering by simulating many random worlds.
Revising a belief in proportion to how much more likely the evidence is under it than under the alternative.
nodes.f: posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio

nodes.t: The belief before the evidence.
How probable the evidence is under a hypothesis.
Error bars calibrated on past errors rather than an assumed distribution; the adaptive version keeps coverage when the world shifts.
Combining rival models with the weights that forecast best out of sample.
Whether multi-period variance grows faster (momentum) or slower (mean reversion) than a random walk (Lo and MacKinlay 1988).
How heavy the tails are; 3 for a bell curve.
Asymmetry of returns; stocks crash down more than they jump up.
The power-law exponent of the tail; below 3 means variance is barely defined for practical purposes.
Ignoring how common something is in general when judging a specific case.
Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please (Kahneman and Tversky 1979).
People judge outcomes as gains and losses from a reference point, overweight small probabilities and feel losses more.
Estimates pulled toward an arbitrary starting number (Tversky and Kahneman 1974).
Believing one knows more than one does; makes people trade too much (Barber and Odean 2000).
Following the crowd because others are; feeds bubbles and crashes.
Buying because prices are rising and others are getting rich.
Overweighting what happened lately.
Assuming recent trends continue; buys high and sells low.
Seeking evidence that agrees with what one already believes.
Selling winners too soon and holding losers too long.
Treating money differently by its label or source.
Believing after the fact that one saw it coming.
Fitting a tidy story to random events.
Believing a run must reverse.
Staying in because of what has already been spent.
Choices changing with how the same facts are presented.
Investors trading on non-information; their sentiment can move prices further than arbitrage can correct (De Long et al. 1990).
Mispricing that persists because correcting it is risky and capital is limited (Shleifer and Vishny 1997).
Soros's loop: prices change fundamentals, which change prices (rising stocks fund more AI capex).
Prices far above any reasonable value, sustained by expectations of further rises; ends in a crash.
A broad speculative frenzy (Kindleberger's Manias, Panics, and Crashes).
When stability has bred enough leverage that a small shock forces a collapse.
Graham's moody business partner who offers prices daily; to be used, not obeyed.
The market's mood; extremes are contrarian signals over months, not days.
Buffett's advice to be fearful when others are greedy and the reverse.
Shares bid up by online retail crowds and short squeezes (2021).
Cheap, volatile shares overpriced for their small chance of a huge gain.
Believing skill governs what chance governs.
Imagining a decision has failed and asking why, before making it (Klein).
Evidence written down in advance that would reverse a decision.
Judging a case by the base rate of similar cases before its details.
The group of similar past cases used for a base rate.
The probability-weighted average outcome; the right target for repeated bets, the wrong one for ruinous ones.
How widely results scatter around expected value; short runs are dominated by it.
The price of a call against the pot; call when equity exceeds call / (pot + call).
Pot odds including what can be won on later streets if the draw hits.
A hand's share of the pot on average against the opponents' range; the engine simulates it.
All the hands an opponent could have given their actions; think in ranges, not single hands.
The value of a bet from the chance opponents fold.
Betting a weak hand so a stronger one folds; in equilibrium, bluffs keep bets credible.
Acting last, with more information; worth money in poker and in markets.
Unintended signals of strength or weakness.
Emotional decision-making after losses; the trader's version is revenge trading.
Keeping each bet small relative to capital so variance cannot end the game.

What legendary and current investors actually said about a question or claim, arranged from extreme bear (-2) to extreme bull (+2): verbatim quotes with speaker, date and source link from a verified library. Never generates a quote.

Run the TLT hedge policy hedge.tlt.v2 on a stock-bond correlation path and a 36-month inflation reading.

Write a structured, hashed order PROPOSAL against the model book and check it against the limits. Never executes: a person reviews it and acts elsewhere.

Score one decision's process (logged before, sized by rule, kill respected, two sources) and its luck quadrant, or a whole journal export: calibration, hit rate, alpha after beta and the process-outcome grid.

Reason over the brain (34 nodes, about 110 links): which root causes explain the readings, what that implies for each holding and the book, which link is most to blame for the misfit, what to observe next, and doing versus seeing a value.

nodes.t: Because passive investors hold the market and earn its return, active investors as a group must also earn the market return before costs. nodes.t: Using survivor-bias-free data, common factors in stock returns, including one-year momentum, plus fund expenses almost fully explain persistence in mutual fund returns. The only strong unexplained persistence is the underperformance of the worst funds, and the results do not support the existence of skilled or informed managers.

nodes.n: Mutual Fund Flows and Performance in Rational Markets

nodes.t: True range is the largest of: today's high minus low, high minus prior close, or low minus prior close (absolute values). ATR, from Wilder (1978), averages true range over 14 periods, then smooths it as (prior ATR x 13 + current TR) / 14. It measures volatility, not direction, and is used for stop and position sizing.

nodes.t: Shows that a gambler with a noisy private wire who bets to maximize the long-run exponential growth rate of capital can grow wealth at a maximum rate equal to the channel's information transmission rate (for fair odds). The origin of the Kelly criterion: bet to maximize expected log wealth.

nodes.n: The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market
nodes.t: Thorp explains that winning requires both positive-expectation bets and correct sizing, and that Kelly sizing maximizes expected log wealth (the growth-optimal strategy). He recounts applying it to blackjack card counting, a sports betting system and securities investing. Chapter 9 of the Handbook of Asset and Liability Management (Elsevier, 2006), first presented in 1997.
nodes.source_title: The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market

nodes.n: Fractional Kelly, overbetting and risk of ruin
nodes.t: Betting c times the Kelly fraction yields c(2 minus c) of the maximum growth rate: half Kelly keeps about 75% of growth with far smaller drawdowns, twice Kelly yields zero long-run growth, and beyond a critical fraction ruin is almost sure. Thorp advises fractional Kelly when edge estimates are uncertain.
nodes.unit: share of full-Kelly growth rate at half Kelly
nodes.source_title: Thorp (2006), The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market, full text (Sections 2, 6, 7.1, 7.4, 8.2)

nodes.n: Thorp partnership returns using Kelly sizing
nodes.t: Thorp reports that his convertible-hedging limited partnership, which used Kelly sizing from November 1969, and its successors compounded at about 20% a year with a standard deviation near 6% and roughly zero correlation to the market. He learned of Kelly from Claude Shannon in 1960 and introduced it to gamblers in Beat the Dealer (1962).

nodes.t: Sets out an axiomatic solution to two-person bargaining: under a small set of reasonableness axioms, the agreed outcome is the one that maximizes the product of the two parties' utility gains over their disagreement point. The foundation of cooperative bargaining theory.

nodes.t: Models bargaining as alternating offers over an infinite horizon with costly delay. Shows there is a unique subgame perfect equilibrium in which agreement is immediate and the split depends on the parties' patience: the more patient side gets more.

nodes.n: BATNA: best alternative to a negotiated agreement
nodes.t: A BATNA is a negotiator's best alternative to a negotiated agreement, that is, what you will do if no deal is reached. It sets whether to accept an offer, how much leverage you hold and when to walk away. The concept comes from Fisher, Ury and Patton's Getting to Yes.

nodes.n: First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus
nodes.t: Across three experiments, whichever side made the first offer, buyer or seller, got a better outcome, and first offers strongly predicted final prices. nodes.n: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
nodes.t: Describes three heuristics people use under uncertainty: representativeness, availability, and adjustment from an anchor. They are efficient but cause systematic, predictable errors; with anchoring, numerical estimates stay biased toward the starting value.

nodes.n: A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix

nodes.t: Proposes a bootstrap for dependent time series that resamples blocks of random, geometrically distributed length, so the resampled series is itself stationary. Widely used to bootstrap returns and Sharpe ratios while keeping autocorrelation.

nodes.n: Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity with Estimates of the Variance of United Kingdom Inflation

nodes.t: Generalizes ARCH so the conditional variance also depends on its own past values (GARCH), giving a parsimonious model of persistent volatility. GARCH(1,1) became the workhorse for forecasting return volatility and risk.

nodes.n: ... and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns

nodes.t: Argues that noise, in the sense of a large number of small events, makes trading in financial markets possible and lets us observe prices. nodes.n: Noise Trader Risk in Financial Markets
nodes.t: Models irrational noise traders whose unpredictable beliefs move prices. Because those beliefs are unpredictable, rational arbitrageurs face risk and cannot bet aggressively against them, so prices can stay far from fundamentals and noise traders can even earn higher expected returns. Helps explain excess volatility and closed-end fund discounts.

nodes.t: Real-world arbitrage takes capital and carries risk, and is done by a small number of specialists using other people's money. As a result arbitrage can fail in extreme situations, when prices move far from fundamentals, and the model predicts where anomalies are likely to persist.

nodes.n: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
nodes.t: Shows that people's choices under risk violate expected utility. People value gains and losses relative to a reference point, with a value function concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses (loss aversion). They underweight probable outcomes versus certain ones and overweight small probabilities.
